Virginia Woolf writes as though consciousness itself is the landscape, and she moves through it the way light moves through water — refracting, never arriving in a straight line. Her sentences breathe in long, subordinate clauses that accumulate sensation before releasing it, then suddenly snap into something brief and stark, almost brutal in its plainness. She reaches perpetually for the interior — not what a character does but what flickers across them while they do it, the half-thought, the memory that surfaces unbidden like a drowned thing. Time is her great obsession and her great distortion; a moment at a window can dilate into years, while decades collapse into a single image of waves or light on a ceiling.

She refuses plot in the conventional sense, refuses the tidy causality of events. What she trusts instead is accumulation — of perception, of mood, of the way one mind brushes against another without ever fully knowing it. Her imagery is sensory and precise: not vaguely poetic but anchored in the physical world, in the colour of a dress, the sound of a clock, the particular quality of an October afternoon. She will use a dash or a parenthetical to open a trapdoor mid-sentence, dropping the reader into a second consciousness before returning, seamlessly, to the first.

The voice carries a kind of melancholy that never tips into self-pity — it is too curious for that, too alive to the comedy of human self-importance. She can be wry, even sharp. But underneath everything runs the elegiac note, the awareness that beauty is inseparable from its passing, that to perceive something fully is already, in some sense, to mourn it.
